messages.author: ac421cf36d1a4c37
messages.subject: Re: Order of variables in zero-order sampling covariance
parts:
I would simply specify a user model that estimates the genetic
correlation of interest. The SE of that rG will then be directly
output. See the STD_genotype portion of the output. This will be based
on the assumption that the h2 is fixed (i.e. it simply standardizes
the covariance relative to th h2, maintaining the p value of the
cov_g).

Alternatively, you can estimate the rG using a model that takes into
account the imprecision of the h2 estimates. This can be done achieved
by specifying a model along the following lines:

'
y1std =~ NA*y1
y2std =~ NA*y2

y1std ~~ 1*y1std
y2std ~~ 1*y2std

y1 ~~ 0*y1
y2 ~~ 0*y2

y1std ~~ y2std
'
In this case, the SE of the rG will not match the SE of cov_g from
S_Stand and perhaps be more similar to what you'd get if resampling
the rG estimates directly with the jackknife.

That said, here is the answer to your question about mapping the
elements of S to V.

On page 3 of the wiki, we show how to get the SEs of each element of S:

k<-nrow(LDSCoutput$S)
SE<-matrix(0, k, k)
SE[lower.tri(SE,diag=TRUE)] <-sqrt(diag(LDSCoutput$V))
In other words, the SEs (in V) corresponding to each element of S can
be mapped back to S by placing them into a matric that is the same
size of S.

We can use this same strategy to simply number each unique element of
S and map it back to the diagonal of V:
k<-nrow(LDSCoutput$S_Stand)
Snum<-matrix(0, k, k)
Snum[lower.tri(Snum,diag=TRUE)] <-1:(k*(k+1)/2)
Snum

To subset out the sampling covariance matrix for parameters of
interest simply refer to the locations of those parameters in V.
For instance, here I am interested in the elements representing the
covariance between variables 1 and 2 with variable 3, so I pull out
the locations within S that they correspond to:
elements=Snum[3,1:2]
Now I subset V based on those elements:
V[elements, elements]

On Sun, Oct 15, 2023 at 9:15 PM ajaynadig wrote:

Hello, and apologies if this is answered elsewhere. I'm interested in using the zero-order covariance matrices from s_ldsc for a delta-method estimator of the variance of the genetic correlation.

My question is: what is the order of variables in these matrices, i.e. sldsc_output$V ? For a two-trait analysis, the columns presumably refer to trait1 heritability, trait2 heritability, and the genetic covariance, where the diagonals are sampling variances and the off-diagonals are the sampling covariances, but it is unclear what the order is.

messages.subject: Re: Order of variables in zero-order sampling covariance
parts:
I misspoke about which approach assumes that h2 is "fixed" and want to correct it for the record.

When you estimate the genetic covariance in genomic SEM and look at the STD_genotype output (which, for a zero-ordered genetic correlation, is the same as looking at the relevant cell of S_Stand and corresponding SE^2 in V_Stand), you are obtaining and estimate and SE that assumes that genetic variances are *random*. In other words, even though the genetic variances are standardized to necessarily be 1.0, they still have SEs because this approach simply rescales the S and V matrices. The p value of the genetic correlation and genetic covariance will therefore match.

The alternative approache, code for which I provided in my last email (also below), specifies factors with *fixed* unit variances and therefore estimates rG in the unstanardized portion of the model itself. These factors are isomorphic with the genetic components of the original GWAS phenotypes, but rescale them to the standardized metric within the undstandardized portion of the model. In this case, the SE of the rG will not match the SE of cov_g from S and V (or from a conventional model that estimates cov_g without specifying factors with unit variances) and is likely to be more similar to what you'd get if resampling the rG estimates directly with the jackknife. In other words, this second approach treats the genetic variances as fixed since they have been rescaled to necessarily be 1.0.

Apologies for the confusion in the previous email.

'
y1std =~ NA*y1
y2std =~ NA*y2

y1std ~~ 1*y1std
y2std ~~ 1*y2std

y1 ~~ 0*y1
y2 ~~ 0*y2

y1std ~~ y2std
'
